findings.question: What are the major semantic topics?
findings.answer: The passages are grouped into eight semantic topics: Computing & mathematics (98 passages), University & student life (87), Language, writing & practice (163), Academic status & conduct (112), History, culture & politics (170), Society, health & policy (138), Natural & molecular science (73), and Credits & degree requirements (118). History, culture & politics is the largest group, followed by Language, writing & practice. Since course descriptions make up a large part of the bulletin, these counts show the composition of the retained corpus rather than which topics are more important to the university.

findings.question: Which topics appear across multiple formal sections?
findings.answer: All eight topics appear in more than one formal section. University & student life appears in 51 sections, Language, writing & practice in 41, and Credits & degree requirements in 33. For example, the credit topic connects Degree Requirements, Entrance Credit and Placement, Transfer of Work Taken Elsewhere, and Study Away. Passage p00057 discusses degree-credit limits, while p00121 discusses transfer-credit limits, showing how similar ideas appear in different parts of the bulletin.

findings.question: Which formal sections contain the most semantically diverse content?
findings.answer: I compare only sections with at least 10 retained passages because a section with just a few passages can look unusually diverse based on very little text. Among these sections, Majors (listed in alphabetical order) is the most diverse, with all eight topics across 60 passages and a Shannon entropy of 2.58 bits. Philosophy follows at 1.81 bits, then Physical Education at 1.69. Shannon entropy uses each topic’s share within a section; zero means one topic, while three bits is the maximum for eight topics. These results still depend on the clustering, and some passages do not fit perfectly into one topic.

findings.question: Which passages from different sections are semantically similar?
findings.answer: Passage p00112 from Entrance Credit and Placement and p00122 from Transfer of Work Taken Elsewhere are each other’s nearest semantic neighbor, with cosine similarity 0.921. Both discuss college work completed before entering DKU, but they focus on different rules. One explains how the credits can count, while the other explains whether the work is eligible for review. This shows that semantically similar passages can appear in different formal sections.

findings.question: Does a search for “credit” occupy one semantic region?
findings.answer: Not completely. Searching for “credit” finds 117 passages across all eight topics. Most are in Credits & degree requirements (73 passages) and Academic status & conduct (29), with smaller numbers in the other topics. The idea of credit is concentrated in a few semantic regions, but it is not limited to one cluster. This is a case-insensitive substring search, so it also matches words such as “credits.”

design: I extracted prose from the 2021–2022 DKU Bulletin using PDF text coordinates and its original outline. Paragraphs retain chapter, section, subsection and page metadata. Cleaning normalizes whitespace, removes exact duplicates and excludes short fragments, tables and reference lists. The overview reports section counts and characteristic TF-IDF terms so readers can see the corpus composition before exploring the map.

Following the lab tasks, I encoded passages with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and normalized the 384-dimensional vectors. Eight long passages were divided into sentence-based chunks, then combined using a normalized, token-weighted mean. UMAP uses 15 neighbors, minimum distance 0.15, cosine distance and seed 401. KMeans uses eight clusters, seed 401 and n_init=auto on the original embeddings. I named topics by inspecting centroid-near passages and characteristic TF-IDF terms; the labels summarize mixed groups rather than official categories.

Each circle represents one passage. Position shows the UMAP projection, color identifies topic, and circle area represents word count. Search and section/topic filters fade nonmatching passages. Zoom and pan reveal crowded neighborhoods. Clicking a point shows its original text, source page and five cosine-nearest passages. A black outline marks the selection; orange outlines mark its neighbors.

The matrix uses color intensity for passage counts. Clicking a cell selects its section and topic; selecting a point outlines the corresponding cell. These linked views reveal how credit policies cross formal boundaries and how major descriptions span many topics. UMAP distances are approximate, topic assignments depend on modeling choices, and counts describe retained prose rather than the entire bulletin.
